items.question: What excited you about machine learning when you were trying to automate stock valuation?
items.object: Machine learning for automating discretionary judgments in stock valuation
items.answer: Near the end of my undergrad, I was taking a class called Value Investing, where they teach you how to value stocks. They give you this template that you're supposed to fill in the inputs and output the value of the stock. I really wanted to automate this process because I'm lazy, but I realized a lot of these inputs that you need you can pull from financial statements and things like that, but some of them are more discretionary: how risky is the business model, how good is the management team, and things like that. Thinking about how one might be able to automate things like this that can't be encoded into rules led me to discover machine learning, and I was just really excited by the possibilities that you can do with the skill set.

items.question: What struck you about Jason Yosinski and Jeff Clune's AI neuroscience talk at Uber?
items.object: Jason Yosinski and Jeff Clune's AI neuroscience talk at Uber
items.answer: I saw a talk by Jason Yosinski and Jeff Clune on AI neuroscience to the Uber audience. items.answer: It comes and goes. That's how I felt that that was something that really attracted me to research: this idea that you kind of just work on things that were intellectually interesting and that you're curious about. At the same time, it is a good middle ground because regardless of whether or not there's follow-up applied value that comes out of your work, it's at least interesting to at least some people. items.question: Why do you find the lottery ticket hypothesis interesting as a way of understanding neural networks?
items.object: The lottery ticket hypothesis
items.answer: The lottery ticket hypothesis states that within a randomly initialized neural network, there exists a subnetwork that, when trained in isolation, can achieve the same performance as the full network with all of the weights. Practically speaking, this means that you can kind of prune the network, have a sparse model, and just train the subnetwork and still get the same performance. I find this really interesting because, one, it suggests that maybe there's some efficiency gains from only having to train a few weights and save on training cost and inference costs. The other reason it's interesting is that it provides a perspective on why overparameterization might be helpful in your networks. The idea is that when you have a lot of parameters, you have more chances of having a lucky subnetwork within that model that just so happens to be a good starting point for this particular task that you're trying to learn on. That's why it's called a lottery ticket: this subnetwork is a lucky initialization, and perhaps that's what's driving the training trajectory of the model when you train the full model.

items.question: What did you want to understand about magnitude pruning in your paper “Deconstructing Lottery Tickets”?
items.object: Magnitude pruning and the research questions behind “Deconstructing Lottery Tickets”
items.answer: The question that we were trying to explore is what is going on here. In the original paper they showed that you can identify these lottery tickets by doing something called magnitude pruning, where you train the full network first and then you keep only the weights that have large magnitude at the end of training. Those constitute your lucky subnetwork. You rewind those weights back to their initialization and train just the subnetwork, and you see that you can achieve the same performance. It opens up a lot of questions, like why this simple method of magnitude pruning is able to identify these lottery tickets, what makes these lottery tickets good for training, and whether other ways of identifying lottery tickets also work.

items.object: The relationship between lottery ticket initialization and pretraining initialization
items.answer: Obviously the lottery ticket initialization is different from one that you might get from pretraining. items.question: What do you mean by the claim that masking a lottery ticket subnetwork is itself a training step?
items.object: Masking as training in lottery ticket subnetworks
items.answer: A really surprising thing we found while doing this investigation is that not only are these subnetworks, these lottery tickets, good at getting to a good final solution when you train them, they're actually already good at initialization before you do any training. If you think about this lottery ticket training procedure, you first train, say, the dense model to convergence, and then you look at the magnitude of the trained weights and set the weights with small magnitudes to zero. You prune those weights, and then for the remaining weights you rewind them back to their initializations. If you just measure this network at initialization after doing this rewinding and pruning, we found that the accuracy is already better than chance. At initialization, the subnetwork is already containing some information about the task. The only thing that we changed is to apply this masking procedure by setting some weights to zero. The interpretation we had was that the weights that we're setting to zero are weights that ended up with a small magnitude if you train the full model. In a way, for these weights, by masking them we're moving them towards the values that they would have gone to anyway if you had trained them. This is what we mean by masking as a training step. It makes sense based on where we're sending the values, and it also makes sense based on the impact that the masking procedure has on the randomly initialized model. It has some interesting implications. One implication is on the hope that maybe we can identify sub networks, or lucky lottery tickets, at initialization without having to do all this expensive training and pruning process. This perspective suggests that you could only find the subnetwork after you've done this training process, because the pruning itself is part of the training. It doesn't preclude the possibility of being able to identify lottery tickets at initialization, but it suggests that maybe this is going to be harder than we think.

items.question: How do you understand the role of the weights that pruning sets to zero in a lottery ticket network?
items.object: The role of weights set to zero during neural network pruning
items.answer: The other interpretation that I think is not very common or intuitive for people is that we typically think of pruning as removing weights that are useless. We're deleting these weights from the network, but our experiments show that the weights that we're sending to zero are not useless; in fact, they are useful at the value of zero. The subnetwork that remains is working alongside the subnetwork that you've set to zero, and they have to be complementary to each other. I think this is why if you randomly reinitialize the weights of the remaining subnetwork, it's not going to work as well, and perhaps why the lottery ticket subnetwork will train to the same basin as the original network. They'll train to a similar solution or solutions that are linearly connected. You can intuitively understand that this is because part of the weights are kind of already locked in, so you're locking into a solution path because all of these weights are now set to zero. I think those are some interesting implications of this perspective of masking as training.

items.question: How do you understand the way individual weights evolve during neural-network training?

items.answer: During training, if you looked at the individual trajectories of weights, they're not going to be monotonically moving towards their final position. If we're thinking of the idea that these weights are moving toward zero, that's not how it happens during the training process. The other thing is these weights are moving toward zero, but they're not actually zero, at least at the end of dense model training, and that maybe changes things. The remaining weights are not going to end up in the exact same values as they were before in the dense model. Individual weights may not have too much meaning, but they're definitely going in different directions throughout training, and you have to do that for the whole network to adjust itself as it trains. There's definitely information being forgotten and relearned throughout training, too. If you look at the performance on an individual data point, you can see that the model could at some point learn to classify this image, but then later on forget again and relearn that. items.question: How do you assess pruning at initialization as a way to identify useful subnetworks for more efficient training?
items.object: Pruning neural networks at initialization to identify useful subnetworks before training
items.answer: There were many papers that tried to do pruning at initialization, maybe by looking at one-step gradient direction of the weight updates and using that information. But then there was a paper that looked at all these proposed methods and compared them to a version where you just shuffle the weights. If you've actually identified a subnetwork that is particularly good, then if you shuffle the weights that should no longer be good. But it turns out that the performance is indistinguishable from some sort of random subnetwork, so that kind of suggested that maybe none of these methods are doing really anything more than something you can do with random pruning, or a clever version of random pruning. I haven't seen anything recently that had better performance on these things, so it seems like maybe this is just a really hard problem, or maybe this is not the easiest way to be doing more efficient training.

items.question: What do you think your study of weight signs and magnitudes reveals about why lottery ticket initialization works?

We found that just keeping the sign was enough to get comparable performance to the full lottery ticket and also the full network, which suggests that what was critical to keep in these subnetworks is just the relative signs; the magnitudes don't matter so much. It's able to get to that solution with just the right sign of the weights, suggesting that maybe the basin of attraction is pretty large and the model isn't super sensitive to perturbations in the initial conditions, or at least this particular form of perturbation, which is changing the magnitude. The idea that the basin of attraction could be pretty large is interesting.

items.question: Why do you find Supermasks interesting as a possible alternative approach to training neural networks?
items.object: Supermasks and searching over subnetworks as an alternative to training neural-network weights

We refer to masks that have this characteristic as Supermasks. It suggests that not only do randomly initialized networks contain subnetworks that are lucky initializations that can train to good performance, they contain subnetworks that are lucky enough to have good performance on your task without any training. Within some randomly initialized network, you can find a subnetwork that performs well already on the task that you're interested in without training the underlying weights. We showed a couple heuristics to identify these Supermasks and one method of actually training and learning to find these masks. It's really interesting because it suggests maybe an alternative approach to training neural networks: instead of training the weights, you can do a search over subnetworks of a randomly initialized model.

items.question: Why do you find the task-specific masking approach in “Supermasks in Superposition” promising for pretrained models?
items.object: The task-specific masking approach in “Supermasks in Superposition”
items.answer: I haven't seen people do this on large language models, but I would love to see it. What I have seen is this really cool paper called “Supermasks in Superposition.” The idea is that they're trying to tackle catastrophic forgetting and continual learning. If you want the model to continuously learn multiple tasks, it tends to forget about the tasks that it learned earlier when it learns a new task. The solution in that paper is basically, you take a pretrained model, maybe trained on a large dataset, and you have downstream tasks that you want to specialize to. Instead of fine-tuning this model to each of those tasks, you find a mask that, when applied to the pretrained model, generates good performance for a downstream task. You can do this because masking is a form of training; it's possible to train a mask toward a different objective. You can have a mask for each of your downstream tasks, and you will never have the issue of catastrophic forgetting because the underlying weights are never changing. At inference time you can have some sort of clever heuristic to identify which mask you should be using. This is cool because maybe the pretrained model has a store of many different features, and by selecting different combinations of these features you can adapt and specialize them to a different task just by choosing a subset of the connections that exist within this model. I'd be excited to see this in large pretrained models, because you can imagine that they have overlapping knowledge about things, but maybe they interfere with each other on a specific downstream task. If you can remove things that are interfering and uncover the right combinations, you can get good downstream performance.

items.question: How do you think forgetting could help artificial neural networks learn better?
items.object: The forget-and-relearn paradigm in artificial neural networks
items.answer: For humans, forgetting, even though it has a bad reputation, is actually a very useful process that our brain does to aid in learning. There's a lot of evidence in cognitive science that shows that forgetting has a symbiotic relationship with learning. The question we were wondering about is: can the same be happening in artificial neural networks as well? We were seeing several different works that do this kind of iterative training procedure to get better generalization or better compositionality, and we tried to figure out if there's some common reason that all of these algorithms that are supposed to be beneficial work. All of them have some speculation for why they work and contribute to better performance, but it's not really proven. We wanted to see if we could unify the picture for all of these different algorithms. The hypothesis we came up with is this forget-and-relearn paradigm, which is a type of training process that comes in stages. It's an iterative process, and in each stage you have a forgetting component and a relearning component. In the forgetting component you try to remove some undesirable information from the model, and in the relearning component you try to retrain the model toward your desired objective. You do this iteratively. The hypothesis is that every time you retrain, you're starting from a better initialization that has less of the undesirable information and more of the desirable information. You can iteratively amplify the desirable information within the model. This can give you a way to steer the model toward desirable characteristics. I'm using these words very loosely, but that is the high-level idea.

items.question: How do you understand why reinitializing and retraining the later layers of a neural network improves its performance?
items.object: Reinitializing and retraining the later layers of a neural network
items.answer: We also have some similar experiments in the paper that don't apply to transfer learning, but do reset the later layers of the network. One of the questions there is: when you reset the later layer, what is causing the improvement after retraining? Is it that you now have a better later layer, because this later layer, let's say the last layer, is now trained on top of better features in the earlier layers, and so you're able to improve the features in that layer through reinitializing and retraining? Or is it the case that the features in the earlier layers are being amplified because they're never reset, so they're continuously being improved every time you do this reinitialization and retraining of the last layer, and those features get stronger and stronger? We set up several experiments to test this, and the answer we concluded was that the second perspective seems to be the right one: the features in the earlier layers are more general and are basically being amplified when they're continuously trained. The signal is propagating back to the earlier layers more than in a fully trained model that has low loss and small gradients. The other subtlety is that when you reinitialize the last layer, you're providing a new environment for the earlier layers to adapt to, and features that are easy to adapt to many of these environments are intuitively more general as well.

items.question: How do you understand the connection between delayed generalization in grokking and forgetting and relearning in neural networks?
items.object: Grokking and its connection to forgetting and relearning
items.answer: I think one perspective is that over this long training, after training accuracy is 100%, the model is basically consolidating or maybe simplifying, or finding the best fit of the solutions that fit the training objective while moving toward some inductive bias that the training procedure has. In grokking there's a delayed generalization behavior: your training accuracy goes up, let's say to 100%, and at this point your test accuracy is still zero or close to zero, so there's no generalization. But if you train for a really long time, suddenly the test accuracy goes up. You can maybe see a double-descent shape of some of the training curves in these experiments. It's constrained by having to still keep a low loss, but it's doing something else. With weight decay, for example, when training loss is low, weight decay will then be primarily responsible for the movement of the weights. In a sense, I can imagine that the network is simplifying during this regime, and you can connect that to the idea of forgetting, removing information that is not critical for doing well on your training set. If you apply the forget-and-relearn procedure to grokking, you do see grokking much faster than with normal training. It's not direct evidence that normal training is doing something similar to forgetting and relearning, but at least both achieve a similar outcome. The connections haven't really been well established, but there are some interesting questions there.

items.question: How has your view of iterative refinement as a way to improve models changed?
items.object: Iterative refinement as a paradigm for improving models
items.answer: I haven't really seen anything that tries to replace an iterative process. I've seen instances where you actually don't need an iterative process: you're able to just forget the right information and you don't have to keep doing this; you can do it in one go. I think it's questionable whether it's a worthwhile investigation to figure out maybe a complicated way of getting at the same benefit, because this is almost another lesson from scaling. The iterative process is taking something that works and just multiplying it, almost bootstrapping the process, and it's easy. We're seeing a lot of examples where, if it works, especially with the absence of clear alternatives, it's actually not that bad. At the time of writing the paper I really didn't like this aspect, but now, even in the large language model field, we're seeing a lot of iterative improvement approaches that I think are really interesting. For example, you have papers that have the model generate some labels for the dataset, then you fine-tune the model on those labels, then generate a new set of labels that are hopefully a little better because the model is better. That's an iterative process, and I think that's actually quite elegant. This is my current feeling about iterative refinement, which is a deeply interesting paradigm for improving models.

items.question: Why do you find in-context learning an exciting way to interact with large language models?
items.object: In-context learning
items.answer: With large language models, what they can do is complete the next tokens, sentences, and paragraphs. You can start the model off with a prompt, or a string of text, and the model is going to complete from that starting point. People have found that you can provide information to the model within this prompt about a task that you want the model to do. One way to do this is to provide a few examples of input and target for this task, append these examples with a test question that you want the model to answer, and the model is seemingly able to pick up how to perform this new task from only seeing what you're providing in context, which is this prompt. That's what people refer to as in-context learning or prompting. I find it exciting because it's a very flexible way of controlling what you're getting out of the model, and you can get the model to perform tasks without changing the underlying weights, so the model itself can stay general and you can interface with it to get new behaviors out of it.

items.question: Why do you describe the prompting approach in your paper “Teaching Algorithmic Reasoning via In-Context Learning” as teaching?
items.object: Teaching algorithmic reasoning through in-context learning
items.answer: In Teaching Algorithmic Reasoning via In-Context Learning, we tried to see if we can get the model to perform algorithmic reasoning by teaching the way to do that through this prompt. The test bed we're using is arithmetic, because it's long been observed that these models are still unable to robustly do simple arithmetic questions, like addition. As the number of digits increase, the model accuracy on these questions will drop. We tried to teach the algorithm for addition by showing the model examples of applying this algorithm and then asking the model to do the same thing. We found that the model is able to generalize out of distribution to questions that are much longer and harder than the examples that we've provided. It's showing that the model is solving this problem using the solution strategy that we've defined for it, which is why we're calling it teaching, although I think that term doesn't sit well with some people because it's in-context learning. items.question: Why do you think teaching a language model the addition algorithm requires such explicit demonstrations?
items.object: Explicit demonstrations for teaching language models the addition algorithm
items.answer: In terms of the actual strategy we use, imagine someone explaining to you how to do addition: you would start with the rightmost digits, add them up, if there's a carry keep track of it, and then move on to the next digits. When you're taught this in school, you're given the actual steps that you need to do and the equations you need to use for each of the digit sums. A lot of times with language models, people don't go into that level of detail because it feels obvious: if I say add up the two numbers, you should know what I mean; if I say keep track of the carry, you should know the carry is one when the sum is greater than ten, zero otherwise. But I think this is assuming a lot about the bias that the model has to interpret these sentences. The idea is to provide as much detail as possible to disambiguate what we mean by each step, so that we can have more robust behavior from the model and get it to do what we want. If you show the addition algorithm by just showing for each step the carry value without explaining how that carry value is derived, then with a limited set of examples there are many valid potential rules that could explain your observations. We can't really fault the model for not doing what we want. We found that when you have very explicit demonstrations, the model is able to pick up on the pattern and flexibly apply it to new situations.

items.question: Why do you find Anthropic’s induction head hypothesis compelling as an explanation of why algorithmic prompting works?
items.object: Anthropic’s induction head hypothesis as an explanation of algorithmic prompting
items.answer: One interpretation I really like is the induction head hypothesis from Anthropic, which says that what is happening in in-context learning is that at the current token output, the model is looking within the context for a pattern that is similar to the pattern that's immediately before the current output, looking at what came next in that previous example, and then outputting something similar. This is what they call an induction head. You can do this in abstract ways; you don't have to find an exact match. You can find a similar match by some sophisticated metric. I really like this, and I think the success of algorithmic prompting, and in particular the importance of having demonstrations and not just descriptions of what you need to do but actually showing it in examples, leverages that idea. We've converted algorithmic reasoning into a pattern-matching question. At each step of the output, the model has to find something in the prompt examples that looks similar, see what happened next, and apply that same relationship. We know models can do this; models are good at pattern matching, and having these demonstrations also makes this process easier per the induction head hypothesis. If you only had instructions, it would require a much more abstract similarity metric to get to the same answer. I like that interpretation because it seems to explain some of why algorithmic prompting is so successful in doing this kind of out-of-distribution generalization.

items.question: How do you understand prompting and fine-tuning as ways of getting the outputs you want from language models?
items.object: Prompting and fine-tuning as ways of constraining LLM outputs
items.answer: For me, the intuitive picture I'm trying to illustrate with algorithmic prompting for what's happening with in-context learning, or prompting, is: how are these models trained? They're trained to output the most likely token given a previous string. When you're training on a large corpus of natural language information, there are many reasonable next tokens that could come, or many reasonable sentences that are maybe equally likely. Maybe what we're doing by providing a prompt is constraining the potential options that make sense, that are likely for the model. Now the model has to output something that's likely given all of this previous information, and that's going to constrain the space of possible outputs. The main goal with interacting with LLMs is how do we make sure that the most likely output per the training distribution is the output that we want from the model? One way we can do that is by providing all this constraining information, so that the model's output has to be consistent with all of this previous information. Another way is fine-tuning, like instruction fine-tuning or RLHF, where you're increasing the likelihood of certain types of outputs from the model. I think all of these are doing this constraining process so that we can get to the spot in the search space that is desirable for us.

items.question: How do you distinguish the goal of algorithmic prompting from algorithm discovery?
items.object: Algorithmic prompting versus algorithm discovery
items.answer: We actually don't make any claims that algorithmic prompting will help with algorithm discovery. I think those are two different problems. The strategy is not meant for discovery; it's meant for robustness and getting out-of-distribution generalization. Algorithm discovery is a much harder problem. So far what we have is just that if you have an algorithm, the model can learn it and apply it, which is a nice first step, but it's not the hard aspect that maybe we want.

items.question: What do you think is missing from current approaches to getting language models to discover algorithms?
items.object: Language models discovering algorithms through hypothesis generation and testing
items.answer: I'm interested in knowing how the model can learn to discover algorithms and generate hypotheses and test them. Maybe the way to do that is by prompting it, but it's not clear. I think some sort of fine-tuning is probably required to get the model into a space where it's coming up with hypotheses. A lot of the work that tries to discover the right solution gets the model to output many possible candidates and does something like majority voting or ensembling of the solutions. That's a really cool process, but it's not enough for what we want; it's not asking the model to generate hypotheses that it can then test. I think there's a gap there between current approaches, which is an interesting research direction.

items.question: What limits of algorithmic prompting are you interested in exploring next?
items.object: The limits of algorithmic prompting
items.answer: I'm interested in pushing the limits of algorithmic prompting and seeing what other types of questions we can solve with this, and where the limits are. Another question I'm interested in is doing reasoning that is not rigid, the way algorithmic reasoning is. That's the one big area this approach doesn't cover: the whole approach for algorithmic prompting relies on this robust and rigid template that a model can follow, so it misses a whole other type of reasoning that we may want. items.question: How do you think the success of scaling large models is changing which machine learning research questions seem worth pursuing?
items.object: The effect of large-model scaling on research agendas and diversity in machine learning
items.answer: I think a lot of PhD students are probably having this crisis of trying to figure out where their research agenda fits in with what's happening in the field, where large models are getting crazy impressive performance. Especially if you were working on things like trying to find failures of existing models and finding tricks or ways of improving them, and you see that all of these failures go away if you just scale, it can bring into question what the most potentially impactful questions are. Those have changed because of what's going on with large models. It is slightly disappointing that there's this convergence of what things are interesting. Maybe that's not the best thing for the field. I think it's always better when people are exploring really different ideas. Compositionality probably will appear with scale, so there's a ton of research that went into that that maybe won't actually be useful going forward.

items.question: Why would you like to see more research on interactions among agents or populations of models?
items.object: Research on interactions and collective intelligence among populations of models
items.answer: As for what's underlooked, I think maybe everything that's not language-model-related is probably underlooked these days. I'm not really well versed in these topics, but I would love to see more studies of interactions between agents or a population of models. That may become really important when we want to apply these things to the real world, where they may need to interact with other humans, or because of the potential of getting more out of collective intelligence of agents or models working together rather than the current paradigm of one giant model that gets bigger and bigger and does everything. Could a population of smaller and maybe more specialized models achieve better output due to collective intelligence dynamics? That's something I think might be interesting and don't see being done very often. Another related but seemingly very important area to study would have to be the human-model interaction component of things.

items.question: How do you view the academic research publishing culture you're navigating as a PhD student?
items.object: Academic research publishing culture and its effects on PhD research
items.answer: I'm not a huge fan of the publishing culture. The number of papers that go on arXiv each day is exploding. There are benefits to getting all of this stuff out there, but there are also a lot of harms. It's hard to find good, useful, and relevant information from the large number of papers being published every day. It's also stressful to be a researcher: now you think you're supposed to write a paper every few months. A lot of PhD students are in this boat where they have to publish papers and get them accepted into conferences in order to graduate, and that's maybe not the right objective or criteria to measure how well you're doing in your PhD. It also encourages working on research that's more short-term and more in line with what most people are interested in, because that's the easiest way to get published, and that's somewhat of a disservice to the scientific field as a whole when people are not encouraged to explore alternative paths. The load on the reviewing process is so large that it's really difficult to get right, and that generates a lot of wasted effort and noise. A lot of this is making the PhD process more and more stressful for people. On the other hand, I also don't like the idea of working on a large project with a large team and keeping it all private and never publishing. That's attractive because you're doing something long-term, but being able to share your findings with the community is the best part, and most fulfilling part for me personally, of being a researcher. Right now I'm trying to find a happy medium where I'm doing some work that helps me advance in my degree, but also trying to keep the motivation for doing things that are just interesting and curious, and maybe not going to be very popular for now but could potentially inspire new ideas. It's definitely a tricky time, and I think maybe a PhD doesn't make sense nowadays for a lot of people for these reasons.

items.question: What do you see as driving the time pressure and pursuit of publication prestige in deep learning research?
items.object: Time pressure and publication prestige in deep learning research
items.answer: I think part of the problem, or maybe two things: one is there are a lot of people doing deep learning research, and the field moves very fast. That gives you time pressure, especially if you're working on stuff that a lot of people are interested in. If you're not done with your project in a reasonable time, someone else would have done it. I don't know how to fix that, because that's inherent in working on a topic that a ton of people are interested in. The prestige thing is an unfortunate byproduct of having a lot of opportunities available, like high-paying jobs or prestigious positions, if you have good publications. That incentivizes people to get their papers reviewed and selected.
